L18@P0: Abstract
L19@P0: The goal of causal representation learning is to find a representation of data that
L20@P0: consists of causally related latent variables. We consider a setup where one has
L21@P0: access to data from multiple domains that potentially share a causal representation.
L22@P0: Crucially, observations in different domains are assumed to be unpaired, that is, we
L23@P0: only observe the marginal distribution in each domain but not their joint distribution.
L24@P0: In this paper, we give sufficient conditions for identifiability of the joint distribution
L25@P0: and the shared causal graph in a linear setup. Identifiability holds if we can uniquely
L26@P0: recover the joint distribution and the shared causal representation from the marginal
L27@P0: distributions in each domain. We transform our results into a practical method to
L28@P0: recover the shared latent causal graph.
L29@P0: 1 Introduction
L30@P0: An important challenge in machine learning is the integration and translation of data across multiple
L31@P0: domains (Zhu et al., 2017; Zhuang et al., 2021). Researchers often have access to large amounts of unpaired data from several domains, e.g., images and text. It is then desirable to learn a probabilistic coupling between the observed marginal distributions that captures the relationship between the domains.
L32@P0: One approach to tackle this problem is to assume that there is a latent representation that is invariant
L33@P0: across the different domains (Bengio et al., 2013; Ericsson et al., 2022). Finding a probabilistic coupling then boils down to learning such a latent representation, that is, learning high-level, latent variables that explain the variation of the data within each domain as well as similarities across domains.
L34@P0: In traditional representation learning, the latent variables are assumed to be statistically independent,
L35@P0: see for example the literature on independent component analysis (Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000; Comon
L36@P0: and Jutten, 2010; Khemakhem et al., 2020). However, the assumption of independence can be too
L37@P0: stringent and a poor match to reality. For example, the presence of clouds and the presence of wet
L38@P0: roads in an image may be dependent, since clouds may cause rain which may in turn cause wet roads.
L39@P0: Thus, it is natural to seek a causal representation, that is, a set of high-level causal variables and
L40@P0: relations among them (Schölkopf et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021b). Figure 1 illustrates the setup of
L41@P0: multi-domain causal representation learning, where multiple domains provide different views on
L42@P0: a shared causal representation.
L43@P0: Our motivation to study multi-domain causal representations comes, in particular, from single-cell
L44@P0: data in biology. Given a population of cells, different technologies such as imaging and sequencing
L45@P0-1: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023).provide different views on the population. Crucially, since these technologies destroy the cells, the
L46@P1: observations are uncoupled, i.e., a specific cell may either be used for imaging or sequencing but not
L47@P1: both. The aim is to integrate the different views on the population to study the underlying causal
L48@P1: mechanisms determining the observed features in various domains (Butler et al., 2018; Stuart et al.,
L49@P1: 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021a; Lopez et al., 2022; Gossi et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2022).
L50@P1: Unpaired multi-domain data also appears in many applications other than single-cell biology. For
L51@P1: example, images of similar objects are captured in different environments (Beery et al., 2018), large
L52@P1: biomedical and neuroimaging data sets are collected in different domains (Miller et al., 2016; Essen
L53@P1: et al., 2013; Shafto et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2003), or stocks are traded in different markets.
L54@P1: In this paper, we study identifiability of the shared causal representation, that is, its uniqueness in
L55@P1: the infinite data limit. Taking on the same perspective as, for example, in Schölkopf et al. (2021)
L56@P1: and Squires et al. (2023), we assume that observed data is generated in two steps. First, the latent
L57@P1: variables Z = (Zi)i∈H are sampled from a distribution PZ, where PZ is determined by an unknown
L58@P1: structural causal model among the latent variables. Then, in each domain e ∈ {1, . . . , m}, the
L59@P1: observed vector Xe ∈ R
L60@P1: de
L61@P1: is the image of a subset of the latent variables under a domain-specific,
L62@P1: injective mixing function ge. That is,
L63@P1: Xe = ge(ZSe),
L64@P1: where Se ⊆ H is a subset of indices. A priori, it is unknown whether a latent variable Zi with
L65@P1: i ∈ Se is shared across domains or domain-specific. Even the number of latent variables which are
L66@P1: shared across domains is unknown. Moreover, we only observe the marginal distribution of each
L67@P1: random vector Xe, but none of the joint distributions over pairs Xe, Xffor e ̸= f. Said differently,
L68@P1: observations across domains are unpaired. Assuming that the structural causal model among the
L69@P1: latent variables as well as the mixing functions are linear, our main contributions are:
L70@P1: 1. We lay out conditions under which we can identify the joint distribution of X1, . . . , Xm.
L71@P1: 2. We give additional conditions under which we are able to identify the causal structure among
L72@P1: the shared latent variables.
L73@P1: In particular, identifiability of the joint distribution across domains enables data translation. That
L74@P1: is, given observation x in domain e, translation to domain f can be achieved by computing
L75@P1: E[Xf |Xe = x]. Furthermore, identifying the causal structure among the shared latent variables lets
L76@P1: us study the effect of interventions on the different domains.
L77@P1: The main challenge in proving rigorous identifiability results for multi-domain data is that we cannot
L78@P1: apply existing results for single-domain data in each domain separately. Even if the causal structure
L79@P1: of the latent variables in a single domain is identifiable, it remains unclear how to combine multiple
L80@P1: causal structures, i.e., in which way latent variables are shared. We circumvent this problem via
L81@P1: a two-step approach: First, we extend the identifiability of linear independent component analysis
L82@P1: (Comon, 1994; Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000; Eriksson and Koivunen, 2004; Mesters and Zwiernik, 2022)
L83@P1: to the multi-domain setup, which allows us to identify the joint distribution and distinguish between
L84@P1: shared and domain-specific latent variables. Moreover, we identify an “overall mixing matrix” and,
L85@P1: in a second step, exploit sparsity constraints in this matrix to identify the causal structure among the
L86@P1: shared latent variables. This leverages recent results on causal discovery under measurement error in
L87@P1: single domains that also exploit sparsity (Xie et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022; Huang
L88@P1: et al., 2022). Although we emphasize that our focus in this paper is on identifiability, our proofs
L89@P1: also suggest methods to learn the joint distribution as well as the shared causal graph from finite
L90@P1: samples. We provide algorithms for the noisy setting and, moreover, we analyze how the number
L91@P1: of domains reduce uncertainty with respect to the learned representation.
L92@P1: The paper is organized as follows. In the next paragraphs we discuss further related work. Section
L93@P1: 2 provides a precise definition of the considered setup. In Section 3 we consider identifiability of
L94@P1: the joint distribution. Using these results, we study identifiability of the causal graph in Section
L95@P1: 4. We conclude with a small simulation study as a proof of concept for the finite sample setting in
L96@P1: Section 5. Due to space constraints, the detailed discussion of the finite sample setting is deferred
L97@P1: to the Appendix. Moreover, the Appendix contains all proofs, discussions on the necessity of our
L98@P1: assumptions, and additional examples and simulation results.
L99@P1: Multi-domain Integration. Motivated by technological developments for measuring different
L100@P1: modalities at single-cell resolution, several methods have been proposed recently for domain

L102@P2: on subsets of the latent variables Zi. The domains may correspond to different data modalities such
L103@P2: as images, text or numerical data. Crucially, the observations across domains are unpaired, i.e., they
L104@P2: arise from different states of the latent causal model.
L105@P2: translation between unpaired data. The proposed methods rely on a variety of techniques, including
L106@P2: manifold alignment (Welch et al., 2017; Amodio and Krishnaswamy, 2018; Liu et al., 2019), matrix
L107@P2: factorization (Duren et al., 2018), correlation analysis (Barkas et al., 2019; Stuart et al., 2019),
L108@P2: coupled autoencoders (Yang and Uhler, 2019), optimal transport (Cao et al., 2022), regression
L109@P2: analysis (Yuan and Duren, 2022), and semisupervised learning (Lin et al., 2022). Implicitly, these
L110@P2: methods presume the existence of a shared latent space where the different modalities either
L111@P2: completely align or at least overlap. However, to the best of our knowledge, none of these methods
L112@P2: have rigorous identifiability guarantees, i.e., the methods are not guaranteed to recover a correct
L113@P2: domain translation mapping even for infinite data. Our work advances the theoretical understanding of
L114@P2: multi-domain integration by providing identifiability guarantees on recovering the shared latent space.
L115@P2: Group Independent Component Analysis. The primary tool that we use for identifiability is
L116@P2: linear independent component analysis (ICA) (Comon, 1994; Eriksson and Koivunen, 2004). Many
L117@P2: works extend ICA to the multi-domain setting. These methods primarily come from computational
L118@P2: neuroscience, where different domains correspond to different subjects or studies. However, to the best
L119@P2: of our knowledge, all prior works require pairing between samples. These works can be categorized
L120@P2: based on whether the samples are assumed to be voxels (Calhoun et al., 2001; Esposito et al., 2005),
L121@P2: time points (Svensén et al., 2002; Varoquaux et al., 2009; Hyvärinen and Ramkumar, 2013), or either
L122@P2: (Beckmann and Smith, 2005; Sui et al., 2009). For reviews, see Calhoun et al. (2009) and Chabriel et al.
L123@P2: (2014). Related are methods for independent vector analysis (Kim et al., 2006; Anderson et al., 2014;
L124@P2: Bhinge et al., 2019) and multiset canonical correlation analysis (Nielsen, 2002; Li et al., 2011; Klami
L125@P2: et al., 2014), which allow the latent variables to take on different values in each domain but still require
L126@P2: sample pairing. Most of the mentioned methods lack identifiability guarantees, only newer work
L127@P2: (Richard et al., 2021) provides sufficient conditions for identifiability. Furthermore, all mentioned
L128@P2: methods assume that every latent variable is shared across all domains, while our setup allows for
L129@P2: shared and domain-specific latent variables. Some methods, e.g., Lukic et al. (2002), Maneshi et al.
L130@P2: (2016), and Pandeva and Forré (2023), permit both shared and domain-specific components, but only
L131@P2: consider the paired setting. In this paper, we extend these results to the unpaired setting.
L132@P2: Latent Structure Discovery. Learning causal structure between latent variables has a long history,
L133@P2: e.g., in measurement models (Silva et al., 2006). One recent line of work studies the problem under
L134@P2: the assumption of access to interventional data (e.g., Liu et al., 2022; Squires et al., 2023). In
L135@P2: particular, Squires et al. (2023) show that the latent graph is identifiable if the interventions are
L136@P2: sufficiently diverse. Another line of work, closer to ours and not based on interventional data, shows
L137@P2: that the graph is identified under certain sparsity assumptions on the mixing functions (Xie et al.,
L138@P2: 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022). However, these methods are not
L139@P2: suitable in our setup since they require paired data in a single domain. One cannot apply them in each
L140@P2: domain separately since it would be unclear how to combine the multiple latent causal graphs, that is,
L141@P2: which of the latent variables are shared. In this work, we lay out sparsity assumptions on the mixing
L142@P2-3: 3functions that are tailored to the unpaired multi-domain setup. The works of Adams et al. (2021) and
L143@P3: Zeng et al. (2021) may be considered closest to ours as they also treat a setting with multiple domains
L144@P3: and unpaired data. However, our setup and results are more general. Adams et al. (2021) assume
L145@P3: that the number of observed variables are the same in each domain, whereas we consider domains
L146@P3: of different dimensions corresponding to the fact that observations may be of very different nature.
L147@P3: Further, we allow for shared and domain-specific latent variables, where the number of shared latent
L148@P3: variables is unknown, while in Adams et al. (2021) it is assumed that all latent variables are shared.
L149@P3: Compared to Zeng et al. (2021), we consider a general but fixed number of observed variables, while
L150@P3: Zeng et al. (2021) only show identifiability of the full model in a setup where the number of observed
L151@P3: variables in each domain increases to infinity. On a more technical level, the conditions in Zeng et al.
L152@P3: (2021) require two pure children to identify the shared latent graph, while we prove identifiability
L153@P3: under the weaker assumption of two partial pure children; see Section 4 for precise definitions.
